title: The Tokyu Hands Edition
summary: On serendipity, retail, and bittersweet closings.
content:
Colin here. Every Tokyo trip has a few fixed points for me, and one has always been the Hands store in Shibuya. (Wedged behind Parco, it’s still known as Tokyu Hands to anyone who’s been going for long enough.) I’d typically walk in to look at another Porter bag I didn’t need, and walk out two hours later with a better pencil sharpener, a card case (for my non-existent business cards), and other distinctly Japanese odds and ends. It was a cabinet of curiosities, and a fun rite of passage for Tokyo visitors.

But this Sunday, November 15, the store will close for good. Its lease is up, and after 48 years, the flagship will be no more. Hands (which the home improvement chain Cainz bought in 2022, dropping the “Tokyu”) will keep nearly 100 other stores, but Shibuya was the idea executed at the highest fidelity, with an estimated 100,000 SKUs unfurling up a hillside, across 24 split levels and 408 steps.

Why is this interesting?

The store started as a real estate problem. Tokyu Land had an awkward, L-shaped, sloping lot where a wooden church once stood, and decided to fill it with a new American import called DIY.

Yet the odd slope forced every floor into staggered A, B and C levels, meaning you corkscrew around the elevator, and soon completely lose track of where you are. In January, the company’s own chairman called it about the hardest building a retailer could work with.

But, like a casino, this disorientation was the part of the charm, and almost matched the overwhelm of the offering. (When it opened in 1978, Hands stocked 1,000 kinds of light bulbs and 3,000 carving chisels, graded from schoolchild to professional.)

Staff wore jeans and aprons, and many came from the trades, so they had a Home Depot-like level of actual understanding of what you might be trying to do. This astonishing depth held to the end, with around 100 nail clippers, 500 shoe care products and more than 1,000 bath salts on the floors this year.

In 2009 Hands named its approach with a slogan: “This is a Hint Market.” The underlying idea is that while a search box like Amazon rewards you for already knowing what you want, the magic of Hands was that it was built for browsing and puttering during the moment before you knew. The serendipity was the juice.

Back in January, celebrating 50 years and its best profits in three decades, Hands gathered journalists inside the Shibuya store to launch a campaign about getting lost on purpose. A pushback against Japan’s obsession with taipa, or time performance, the pitch was to wander and savor the time you were spending. But then, four months later, the closure notice came.

On October 29, a crane went up to the big green sign, and HANDS became THANKS, with the old Tokyu-era hand logo pulled out of retirement. Inside, staff built the main thank-you poster from strips of masking tape. The run of 48 thank-yous includes one to the skip floors, for getting everybody lost. (CJN)
